Task and constraints: Count decodings of a digit string with '*' wildcards, modulo 10^9+7.
Idea: Use a three-slot rolling DP for single-character and two-character decoding contributions.
Technique and why it applies: A '*' has nine single-digit choices. Two-character combinations depend on the preceding symbol: '1*' contributes nine, '2*' six, and '**' fifteen. The three slots preserve dp[i], dp[i-1], and dp[i-2].
Invariant: dp[(i+1)%3] stores the number of ways to decode the prefix through position i.
Edge cases: The code accesses s[0], so empty strings fail; problem inputs are nonempty. Every transition is reduced modulo M, but the initial dp[1] is not explicitly reduced because it is at most nine.
Complexity: One pass gives O(n) time and the rolling array uses O(1) space. Author labels are correct.

Task and constraints: Find the duplicated value and the missing value in a permutation of 1 through n with one error.
Idea: Count occurrences in an array indexed by each value, then identify the count-two and count-zero entries.
Technique and why it applies: v[num] records the frequency of each value. Scanning indices 1 through n identifies the duplicate and missing values directly.
Invariant: After the first pass, v[i] equals the number of times value i occurs in nums.
Edge cases: The expected input has exactly one duplicate and one missing number. Values outside 1..n would cause an indexing error or corrupt the frequency table.
Complexity: Both passes take O(n) time and the frequency array uses O(n) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Find the longest chain of pairs where each pair's second value is strictly less than the next pair's first value.
Idea: Sort pairs by their ending coordinate and greedily select every pair that begins after the last selected pair ends.
Technique and why it applies: Choosing the earliest finishing pair leaves the most room for later pairs. i stores the index of the last selected pair, and cnt tracks how many have been selected.
Invariant: The selected chain is compatible, and the end of its last pair is as early as possible among chains of the same length.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero because the loop is skipped. The strict comparison pairs[i][1] < pairs[j][0] enforces the required non-overlap.
Complexity: Sorting costs O(n log n), then one scan takes O(n), with O(1) auxiliary variables beyond sorting. Author labels are conventional.

Task and constraints: Count all palindromic substrings in s, counting occurrences at different positions separately.
Idea: Apply Manacher's algorithm to a transformed string with separators, then sum the palindrome radii contributions.
Technique and why it applies: Inserting '#' between characters lets odd and even palindromes share one radius representation. C and R track the current rightmost palindrome; mirror radii seed expansions, and each radius contributes (radius+1)//2 original substrings.
Invariant: P[i] is the palindrome radius around transformed position i, while C and R describe the rightmost known palindrome.
Edge cases: Empty input transforms to '^##$' and produces zero contributions. Sentinel characters prevent expansion beyond the transformed string under the algorithm's assumptions.
Complexity: The radius expansion is amortized O(n) time and P uses O(n) space, matching author labels.

Task and constraints: Replace each word in a sentence with the shortest dictionary root that is its prefix, if one exists.
Idea: Build a trie of roots and walk each word until a terminal root is reached or the path fails.
Technique and why it applies: Each dictionary word marks its final trie node with '_end'. During replacement, the first terminal node encountered gives the shortest matching root; otherwise the original word is kept.
Invariant: The trie represents all dictionary roots, and replace scans each word from its first character to the earliest terminal prefix.
Edge cases: Words with no root prefix remain unchanged. sentence.split() collapses whitespace, so the output normalizes spacing to single spaces. The reduce expression builds trie paths by repeated dictionary indexing.
Complexity: Trie construction and sentence traversal are O(total characters) expected time, with O(total dictionary characters) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Predict which senate party will win when senators may ban one opposing senator per turn.
Idea: Store the original indices of Radiant and Dire senators in separate queues and repeatedly compare the earliest active senator from each side.
Technique and why it applies: The senator with the smaller index acts first and bans the opponent, then is requeued at index+n to represent their next turn in the following round.
Invariant: Each queue contains the future turn order of senators still active for that party.
Edge cases: When either queue becomes empty, the other party wins. The queue method handles wraparound without rebuilding the senate string.
Complexity: Each senator is dequeued and requeued once per round in which they survive, giving O(n) total time and O(n) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return the winning party in the Dota2 Senate banning process.
Idea: Maintain queues of Radiant and Dire indices, repeatedly allowing the earlier index to ban the later one.
Technique and why it applies: The surviving senator is appended with index+n so its next turn is ordered after the current round. This simulates cyclic turn order using increasing integer timestamps.
Invariant: Queue entries preserve the relative future order of surviving senators; the party with a nonempty queue at the end wins.
Edge cases: If the senate contains only one party, the loop never runs and that party is returned. The final length comparison is equivalent to checking which queue remains nonempty.
Complexity: Each senator is requeued until banned; total queue operations are O(n), with O(n) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum number of copy-all and paste operations needed to create n 'A' characters.
Idea: Memoize recursive states defined by clipboard size and current screen size, considering copy and paste actions.
Technique and why it applies: Pasting adds the clipboard count to the screen. Copying is considered when the screen is larger than the clipboard, and each action costs one operation. Overshooting n is treated as impossible.
Invariant: memo[(clipboard_count,screen_count)] stores the minimum remaining operations from that state to reach exactly n.
Edge cases: n=1 returns zero. The copy condition is a pruning rule intended to avoid redundant copy actions; memoization limits repeated states.
Complexity: The state space is bounded by combinations of screen and clipboard counts up to n, so worst-case time and space can be O(n²), with recursion depth O(n). No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Compute the minimum copy/paste operations needed to build n copies of 'A'.
Idea: Factor n into primes and sum those prime factors with multiplicity.
Technique and why it applies: Building a multiple by a factor p requires one copy operation and p-1 pastes, costing p operations. A prime factorization decomposes the optimal construction into these costs.
Invariant: result accumulates the operation cost for every prime factor removed from n.
Edge cases: n=1 returns zero because no factor is found. The trial divisor p increments one by one, testing factors through the square root of the remaining n.
Complexity: Trial division is O(sqrt(n)) time in the usual bound and O(1) auxiliary space, matching author labels.

Task and constraints: Determine whether a sequence of U, D, L, and R moves returns the robot to its origin.
Idea: Count the move letters and verify that up/down and left/right counts balance.
Technique and why it applies: Vertical displacement is zero when U and D counts match; horizontal displacement is zero when L and R counts match. Both equalities are required for the final position to be the origin.
Invariant: Counter(moves) records how many times each direction occurs in the sequence.
Edge cases: An empty move string would return True. Counter is referenced but not imported in the shown snippet, so it must be defined externally.
Complexity: Counting the moves takes O(n) expected time and O(u) space for the four possible directions. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Determine whether a robot's move sequence ends at its starting position.
Idea: Track vertical and horizontal displacement directly while scanning the moves.
Technique and why it applies: U and D adjust the vertical coordinate by opposite units; R and L do the same for horizontal position. Both coordinates must return to zero.
Invariant: v and h equal the net vertical and horizontal displacements after the processed prefix.
Edge cases: Empty input leaves both coordinates zero and returns True. Unrecognized characters are ignored, relying on the move alphabet constraint.
Complexity: The scan is O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space, matching author labels.

Task and constraints: Return the k closest values to x from a sorted array, with the output sorted ascending.
Idea: Compute each value's distance from x, select the k smallest distance records with a heap helper, then sort their values.
Technique and why it applies: Each record stores the original index and absolute distance. nsmallest selects the nearest records; the indices recover values from arr and the final sort restores ascending order.
Invariant: distances contains one candidate record per array element, and result contains the selected values before final sorting.
Edge cases: The code references heapq without importing it in the shown snippet. Ties by distance are not explicitly broken by value, so the selected set may violate the problem's smaller-value tie rule.
Complexity: Building records is O(n), selecting k is typically O(n log k), and sorting output is O(k log k). Storage is O(n) for distances. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Find the k elements closest to x in sorted arr, returning them in sorted order.
Idea: Binary-search the insertion point of x, then expand a window left or right based on which next candidate is closer.
Technique and why it applies: The array's sorted order means the nearest candidates are adjacent to the insertion point. Equal distances choose the left element through <=, implementing the smaller-value tie-break.
Invariant: [left+1,right) is the selected window, and each iteration expands it by exactly one element.
Edge cases: x outside the array is handled by boundary conditions. k=0 returns an empty slice. The code assumes arr has enough elements to select k.
Complexity: Binary search is O(log n), followed by k expansions, giving O(log n+k) time and O(1) auxiliary space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Decide whether a sorted array can be partitioned into consecutive increasing subsequences, each of length at least three.
Idea: Count remaining occurrences and track how many valid subsequences end at each value.
Technique and why it applies: A value is first used to extend a subsequence ending at num-1; if none exists, the code starts a new subsequence using num,num+1,num+2 when available. Failure of both choices returns False.
Invariant: count stores unused occurrences and tails records the number of subsequences currently ending at each value.
Edge cases: Arrays shorter than three return False. The code uses defaultdict imported as a class attribute, then references it in the method; name resolution may fail because it is not bound in the method's global scope.
Complexity: Counting and processing are O(n) expected time and O(n) space for the two maps. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Check whether nums can be split into consecutive subsequences of length at least three.
Idea: Process equal-value runs and maintain counts of subsequences of lengths one, two, and at least three ending at the previous value.
Technique and why it applies: If values are consecutive, existing length-one and length-two subsequences must be extended first. Extra copies can start new subsequences; otherwise the method returns False. A gap requires all short subsequences to have been completed.
Invariant: cnt1, cnt2, and cnt3 count active subsequences ending at pre with the respective lengths/categories.
Edge cases: A gap is invalid if cnt1 or cnt2 remains nonzero. At the end, only cnt1==0 and cnt2==0 is required because length-three-or-more subsequences are valid.
Complexity: The sorted array is scanned once with constant state, giving O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space. Author labels are correct.

Task and constraints: Smooth each image pixel by replacing it with the floor of the average of valid cells in its surrounding 3×3 neighborhood.
Idea: For each cell, compute bounded row and column ranges and average the included pixel values.
Technique and why it applies: max/min bounds clip the neighborhood at image edges. The nested loops sum valid cells and count them; integer division floors the average as required.
Invariant: avg(i,j) returns the floor average of all original image values in the clipped neighborhood around (i,j).
Edge cases: Corner and edge cells use fewer than nine values. The code assumes img is nonempty and has at least one column.
Complexity: Each output cell examines at most nine input cells, giving O(mn) time and O(mn) output space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum number of turns a strange printer needs to print string s, where one turn prints one character over a contiguous interval.
Idea: Remove adjacent duplicate characters, then memoize interval states that also record the background character already printed across the interval.
Technique and why it applies: Matching endpoint characters can share a print turn. Otherwise, the recurrence tries positions carrying the left character and splits the interval to combine turns.
Invariant: _dp(i,j,background) is intended to be the minimum additional turns to realize s[i:j+1] given the surrounding background.
Edge cases: Empty strings return zero through the i>j base case. lru_cache is not used; the explicit dictionary _m caches states. The background optimization makes this recurrence more intricate than standard interval DP.
Complexity: The memo state includes interval endpoints and a character background, with up to O(n²·alphabet) states and O(n) split work per state; O(n³) or higher depending on alphabet is plausible. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Compute the minimum number of printer turns needed to print the string, where one turn prints one character over a continuous range.
Idea: Use interval DP and try to merge the final character's printing turn with earlier occurrences of the same character.
Technique and why it applies: The baseline prints s[j] separately after solving [i,j-1]. If s[k] equals s[j], one turn can cover both positions, combining the solution for [i,k] with the middle interval [k+1,j-1].
Invariant: lookup[(i,j)] stores the minimum turns for substring s[i:j+1].
Edge cases: Empty intervals return zero, and empty input therefore returns zero. The recurrence skips candidate k positions whose character differs from s[j].
Complexity: There are O(n²) intervals and up to O(n) split candidates per interval, giving O(n³) time and O(n²) memo space, matching the author labels.

Task and constraints: Determine whether the array can become non-decreasing by modifying at most one element.
Idea: Scan adjacent pairs, count descents, and adjust one side of the first descent based on the preceding value.
Technique and why it applies: If nums[i-2] <= nums[i], lowering nums[i-1] is safe; otherwise raising nums[i] to nums[i-1] preserves the earlier order. A second descent means one modification is insufficient.
Invariant: unstable counts descents encountered, and the array is modified locally to preserve non-decreasing order when possible.
Edge cases: A descent at i=1 can always be fixed by lowering the first element. The method mutates nums. Empty or single-element arrays return True.
Complexity: The scan is O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space. No labels were supplied.
